## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kūṭadanta Sutta* is the fifth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya*. Named after its primary interlocutor, the wealthy and learned brahmin Kūṭadanta [Ling 1968; Ham 2016], the text is constructed as a frame story containing an embedded past-life narrative (*jātaka*) [Keown 2006; Fenn 1994; Winternitz 1933]. In the frame story, Kūṭadanta prepares to perform an elaborate animal sacrifice and, despite objections from other brahmins who enumerate his high status and Vedic learning, visits the Buddha to inquire how best to carry it out [Ham 2016; Anālayo 2017]. In response, the Buddha relates the legend of King Mahāvijita, whose chaplain advised him to substitute violent sacrificial slaughter with socio-economic welfare and support for the realm's citizens, emphasizing reciprocity between monarch and subjects [Fenn 1994; Winternitz 1933]. Moving beyond non-violent material offerings, the Buddha then delineates a hierarchy of higher spiritual sacrifices, culminating in the renunciatory monastic life, moral conduct, and ultimate liberation [Chung 2012].

Regarding the embedded narrative, the Pali text identifies the Bodhisatta with the brahmin chaplain, while its Chinese counterpart identifies him with the king, and Sanskrit fragments identify him with both [Anālayo 2011]. The discourse has an established full parallel in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 23, *Jiùluótántóu-jīng* 究羅檀頭經), which has been translated and analyzed by Konrad Meisig, as well as surviving Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 30; SF 52) [Meisig 2010; Bingenheimer 2018]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text sharing with discourses such as the *Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta* (DN 4) and *Caṅkī Sutta* (MN 95), along with Vinaya Khandhaka passages [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language matches computed by DharmaNexus confirm alignments with DĀ 23 as well as sections in the Tibetan *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* and Sanskrit Vinaya literature [DharmaNexus]. The text is also cited in early canonical Abhidhamma and exegetical works including the *Kathāvatthu* and *Mahāniddesa*.
